title: What should you ask first in a valuation case, and which trap should you avoid?
description: The first question to ask in a valuation case, how to structure it, and the trap to avoid.
hook: Valuation questions ask what something is worth. You will not need a spreadsheet, just a clear way of thinking about value.
body:
The first question to ask

Valuing a standalone business or a stream of cash flows?

How to build your structure

  • Discounted cash flow (DCF): future cash flows, discounted to today
  • Trading comparables: what similar listed companies are worth, e.g. price to earnings or EV to EBITDA
  • Transaction comparables: what similar companies sold for
  • Use at least two methods and compare

The trap most people fall into

Adding up future years without discounting.

For the full tree, with every branch, read the acquisition (M&A) framework.

Worked example: enterprise value is not equity value

A business generates £10 million of annual EBITDA, and similar companies trade around 8× EBITDA. A quick enterprise-value estimate is £80 million. If the company has £25 million of debt and £5 million of cash, a simplified equity-value estimate is £80 million − £25 million + £5 million = £60 million. This assumes no material non-operating adjustments or other debt-like items.

Now sense-check with cash flow. A company needing heavy equipment replacement may turn much less of its EBITDA into free cash flow than a software business with the same EBITDA. An 8× multiple therefore cannot stand alone. Build an independent estimate using future free cash flow, a reasonable discount rate and a terminal value.

Be explicit about your output: an estimated value range, the assumptions that drive it, and what evidence would change it. Never combine a debt-inclusive enterprise value with an equity earnings multiple, and do not present a peer multiple as an objective fact when it is merely an assumption.
